title: Rattan Singh Bhangu
hook: his Panth Prakash told the Khalsa's hard century in verse

segments.voice: Yesterday, the three roads: Sikh chroniclers, Persian records, and memory. Your line was how do we know. Today, one of those chroniclers, by name.

A Sikh sits down to write. Not in prose. In verse, line after line that can be read aloud and remembered. He has the stories his family told him: the riders and the forests, the great killing, the temple blown up and rebuilt. Some of them are about his own family. And, by his own account, he has a reason to write: outsiders are asking about the Sikhs, and he wants the Sikh side told by a Sikh.
screen: `A SIKH WRITES IN VERSE.` → `STORIES HIS FAMILY TOLD HIM.` → `THE SIKH SIDE, TOLD BY A SIKH.`

segments.voice: First, the book. It's called Panth Prakash. Panth is the path, and the word Sikhs use for the whole community. Prakash is light, the shining of something into view. So the title promises to bring the Panth into the light. Second, why he wrote it. Bhangu says a British officer was collecting accounts of Sikh history, and that he heard the Sikhs described by people who didn't know them. So he set out to tell it from inside. That's a choice worth noticing. He didn't write an angry reply. He wrote the long story, with names, places and family memory, so it would be there for anyone who asked. Third, his family is in it. Bhangu traces his line to Mehtab Singh, one of the riders remembered for punishing the man who had turned the Harmandir into a place of drinking and dancing. So when he tells the hard century, he's telling his own family's world. Fourth, how to read him. Because he wrote later, from memory and family tradition, historians read him carefully, beside other sources: yesterday's lesson in action. And yet several stories on this path in recent weeks, Kapur Singh fanning the sangat, the boy Jassa Singh singing, the shaheedi bunga, are told in the forms Sikhs know through tellings like his. When this path says tradition says, Bhangu is one of the voices in that tradition. The chronicler.
screen: `PANTH PRAKASH: THE PATH BROUGHT TO LIGHT.` · `WRITTEN SO THE SIKH SIDE WAS TOLD.` · `HIS OWN FAMILY IN THE STORY.` · `READ CAREFULLY, AND STILL TREASURED.` · then, large: `THE CHRONICLER.`

segments.voice: Find or recall one line of history, a sentence from a book, a plaque on a building, an inscription on a gravestone, the first line of a page about where your family came from, and read it slowly, once. Then put it down, breathe, and ask who wrote it, and where they were standing. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.
Bhangu. The Sikh chronicler whose Panth Prakash told the Khalsa's hard century in verse, from family memory, so the Sikh side would be told. Today's word.
Your line: the chronicler. Every story you love was kept by someone. Day eight hundred seventy-six, and counting.
